title: End-to-End Guarantees for Masked Diffusion Models under Conditional Mixing

paper.title: End-to-End Guarantees for Masked Diffusion Models under Conditional Mixing
paper.abstract: Abstract Masked diffusion models train a denoiser on masked cross-entropy and generate by unmasking many positions in parallel. Existing MDM sampling bounds assume an exact denoiser or leave its error uncontrolled while training bounds cover only the masking distribution on which the model was trained. We present an end-to-end guarantee for a learned denoiser under conditional mixing (CM): stationary sources (e.g. floored order- r r Markov and two-sided-Doeblin hidden-Markov sources) for which revealing distant visible tokens moves a masked token’s posterior on average exponentially little in the distance with correlation length τ c \tau_{c} . We show the empirical risk minimizer trained under any masking distribution attains per-token excess ε ′ \varepsilon^{\prime} on that distribution from ε ′ − 𝒪 ⁡ ( τ c ​ log ⁡ | 𝒱 | ) \varepsilon^{\prime-\mathcal{O}(\tau_{c}\log|\mathcal{V}|)} training sequences, independent of sequence length N N — one sample budget serves every decoding schedule when each schedule’s denoiser is trained under its own weighting. We further show that the exponent’s order Θ ⁡ ( τ c ​ log ⁡ | 𝒱 | ) \Theta(\tau_{c}\log|\mathcal{V}|) is minimax-optimal up to constants; more efficient rates require added structure. With this, we bound the end-to-end KL as KL ( π ∥ p alg ) ≤ ε + N ε ′ \KL(\pi\|p_{\mathrm{alg}})\leq\varepsilon+N\varepsilon^{\prime} under a dilated schedule of T = 𝒪 ⁡ ( τ c ​ log ⁡ ( N ​ | 𝒱 | / ε ) ) T=\mathcal{O}(\tau_{c}\log(N|\mathcal{V}|/\varepsilon)) denoising steps versus Ω ⁡ ( N ) \Omega(N) steps for a fixed random order on an explicit CM source. Finally, we show that block-autoregressive samplers chain across blocks with no added error and that a Λ \Lambda -looped order- r r message-passing class on order- r r sources achieves polynomial sample complexity, with approximation error improving per loop until saturation at Λ ​ r ≈ τ c ​ log ⁡ ( 1 / ε ′ ) \Lambda r\approx\tau_{c}\log(1/\varepsilon^{\prime}) . Experiments on released and retrained models support our results’ qualitative predictions.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text:
Masked diffusion language models (MDMs) trade the autoregressive factorization for per-step conditional independence between tokens, which lets them generate many tokens in parallel. MDMs use an absorbing-state/masked forward process on tokens ( Austin et al., 2021 ; Campbell et al., 2022 ; Shi et al., 2024 ; Sahoo et al., 2024 ) and generate by unmasking several positions per step. Discrete diffusion training theory and sampling theory have largely developed separately. On the sampling side, recent work bounds the convergence and step count of the reverse process ( Zhang et al., 2025 ; Chen and Ying, 2025 ; Liang et al., 2025 ; Liang et al., 2026 ) , gives information-theoretic accounts of the factorization error ( Li and Cai, 2025 ; Lavenant and Zanella, 2025 ; Dmitriev et al., 2026 ) , limits for parallel generation ( Chen et al., 2026 ) , and analyses of confidence-adaptive decoding ( Cai and Li, 2026 ) . Every result assumes an exact denoiser or leaves the denoiser’s error at the masking patterns that decoding visits as a free parameter. On the training side, finite-sample bounds exist for generative masked language modeling ( Li et al., 2024 ) and discrete diffusion score estimation ( Srikanth et al., 2026 ; Cho and Wu, 2026 ) ; these control the learned model at the masking distribution on which it was trained and compose it with a matched sampler (Gibbs-style chains or CTMC samplers). Without structural assumptions, their rates scale with the full state space | 𝒱 | N |\mathcal{V}|^{N} ( Cho and Wu, 2026 ) . Composing training with the parallel-sampling decompositions above requires a bound covering the masking patterns of an arbitrary decoding strategy with a per-token sample budget independent of the strategy and N N ; no existing result provides one. We provide such a bound for stationary data whose token-to-token influence on average decays exponentially with distance, a source family we call conditional mixing ( Assumption 1 ), which covers finite-order Markov sources with a transition floor (e.g. smoothed n n -grams) and hidden Markov sources whose hidden kernel satisfies a two-sided Doeblin condition. sections.heading: Learning the denoiser.
sections.text: The learning results cited in Section 1 hold at the training masking distribution. Our bound holds at every masking distribution with one per-token budget that does not depend on N N , provided the denoiser is trained under the decoding schedule’s weighting ( Theorem 1 ). Its window argument extends short-memory prediction ( Sharan et al., 2018 ) from one-sided to two-sided conditionals under arbitrary masks. Its lower bound ( Theorem 2 ) parallels minimax rates for predicting Markov chains ( Hao et al., 2018 ; Han et al., 2023 ) and hidden Markov models ( Han et al., 2024 ) .

sections.heading: Composing learning with sampling.
sections.text: We use the decomposition of Lavenant and Zanella (2025) , which splits the sampler’s KL into a learning term and the factorization error. Earlier end-to-end results pair the learned model with a sampler matched to its training distribution ( Li et al., 2024 ; Cho and Wu, 2026 ) . Corollary 1 pairs it with any non-adaptive decoding strategy, including parallel ones, and with adaptive strategies under strong conditional mixing.

sections.heading: Parallel decoding.
sections.text: With exact conditionals, the KL of a deterministic adaptive decoding policy equals its accumulated conditional total correlation ( Ben-Hamu et al., 2025 ) , and order- r r Markov chains admit exact schedules with r ⁡ ( ⌈ log 2 ⁡ ( N / r ) ⌉ + 1 ) r(\lceil\log_{2}(N/r)\rceil+1) steps ( Wen et al., 2026 ) . For random walks on graphs, a bisection sampler is exact in logarithmically many steps ( Bansal et al., 2026 ) . On order- r r sources our dilated schedule uses 𝒪 ⁡ ( τ c ​ log ⁡ N ) \mathcal{O}(\tau_{c}\log N) steps with τ c ≤ r / ( 2 ​ q min r ) \tau_{c}\leq r/(2q_{\min}^{r}) ( Proposition 1 ). It needs only conditional mixing, which includes Doeblin hidden Markov sources, and it works with a learned denoiser. Under Dobrushin-type conditions, parallel Markov chain Monte Carlo samples Gibbs distributions in 𝒪 ⁡ ( log ⁡ N ) \mathcal{O}(\log N) parallel rounds ( Liu and Yin, 2022 ) , and the LOCAL algorithm of Feng et al. (2017) needs an extra factor of the maximum degree.

sections.heading: Mixing conditions.
sections.text: Conditional mixing adapts strong spatial mixing ( Weitz, 2006 ) to masked prediction and averages it over the source ( Section 3 ). Our hidden Markov result ( Proposition 2 ) extends filter stability under a mixing kernel ( Le Gland and Oudjane, 2004 ; Atar and Zeitouni, 1997 ) to two-sided conditionals under arbitrary masks.

sections.heading: 8 Discussion
sections.text: We present an end-to-end KL bound for masked diffusion with a learned denoiser under conditional mixing. The sample budget is the same for every decoding schedule and minimax-optimal in its exponent’s order, and we specialize the bound to dilated and block-autoregressive decoding and to a looped message-passing class on order- r r sources. Dilated decoding reaches KL ε + N ​ ε ′ \varepsilon+N\varepsilon^{\prime} in 𝒪 ⁡ ( τ c ​ log ⁡ ( N ​ | 𝒱 | / ε ) ) \mathcal{O}(\tau_{c}\log(N|\mathcal{V}|/\varepsilon)) steps, where a fixed random order needs Ω ⁡ ( N ) \Omega(N) on an explicit source, and released and finetuned models show the same ordering. The guarantee holds for a denoiser trained under the decoding weighting, and its training term enters per token, so the sequence-level budget grows polynomially in N N . Text with power-law pairwise mutual information lies outside conditional mixing, and for such sources dilated decoding needs polynomially many steps ( Remark 1 ). Future work includes bounds for slower-mixing sources, schedules that avoid the context-free first step, tighter constants, influence probes on larger MDMs, and samplers that revise decoded tokens ( Liu et al., 2025 ; Zhao et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025 ) .

sections.heading: Appendix A Proofs
sections.text: We prove the two theorems presented in the paper with the help of a few observations about how distant tokens affect Markov-structured data and motivates our conditional mixing assumption as well as how much information we lose by ignoring certain distant tokens. We structure Appendix A by first proving in Section A.1 the lemmas and bounds that we use in our theorem proofs, analyzing in Section A.2 conditional mixing for finite-order and hidden Markov sources, connecting the sampler’s learning error to excess risk in Section A.3 , and finally proving our main learning and decoding results in Sections A.4 and A.5 .

Experiments on released and retrained models support our results’ qualitative predictions. 1 Introduction Masked diffusion language models (MDMs) trade the autoregressive factorization for per-step conditional independence between tokens, which lets them generate many tokens in parallel. MDMs use an absorbing-state/masked forward process on tokens ( Austin et al., 2021 ; Campbell et al., 2022 ; Shi et al., 2024 ; Sahoo et al., 2024 ) and generate by unmasking several positions per step. Discrete diffusion training theory and sampling theory have largely developed separately. On the sampling side, recent work bounds the convergence and step count of the reverse process ( Zhang et al., 2025 ; Chen and Ying, 2025 ; Liang et al., 2025 ; Liang et al., 2026 ) , gives information-theoretic accounts of the factorization error ( Li and Cai, 2025 ; Lavenant and Zanella, 2025 ; Dmitriev et al., 2026 ) , limits for parallel generation ( Chen et al., 2026 ) , and analyses of confidence-adaptive decoding ( Cai and Li, 2026 ) . Every result assumes an exact denoiser or leaves the denoiser’s error at the masking patterns that decoding visits as a free parameter. On the training side, finite-sample bounds exist for generative masked language modeling ( Li et al., 2024 ) and discrete diffusion score estimation ( Srikanth et al., 2026 ; Cho and Wu, 2026 ) ; these control the learned model at the masking distribution on which it was trained and compose it with a matched sampler (Gibbs-style chains or CTMC samplers). Without structural assumptions, their rates scale with the full state space | 𝒱 | N |\mathcal{V}|^{N} ( Cho and Wu, 2026 ) .
